scenes.visual: Title card 'Eight Females from Texas' over a map outline of southern Florida. COLOUR MAP, same in both films: thin BLUE lines = population runs, plotted as log numbers (y) against years (x); RED-ORANGE dashed line = the floor; GOLD arrow = the trend; grey jitter band = the swings. Film 2 adds TEAL = Florida ancestry, PURPLE = Texas ancestry, TEAL-PURPLE stripes = admixed. Cream background, 16:9. Numbers appear only as on-screen text. Runs and fractions are computed from a random walk on log numbers (trend and swings as labelled, floor 10 animals) and labelled 'computed'; anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: A model that holds survival fixed can miss something. If inbreeding keeps building, survival or fertility can fall, and the trend tilts down. Can adding new genes tilt it back up?
scenes.visual: A quick link from the text: the first film's chart, one blue run with the gold arrow tilting downward toward the red-orange floor, a small tag 'survival held fixed?' crossed out, and the vortex loop small in a corner.
scenes.narration: A model that holds survival fixed can miss something. If inbreeding keeps building, survival or fertility can fall, and the trend tilts down. Can adding new genes tilt it back up?

scenes.tts: Southern Florida held a small, isolated population of Florida panthers. Its animals showed signs linked to inbreeding: kinked tails, heart defects and poor sperm.
scenes.visual: Map of southern Florida with a small TEAL patch, label 'Florida panthers, small and isolated'. A cartoon panther with three callout tags: 'kinked tail', 'heart defects', 'poor sperm'. Schematic.
scenes.narration: Southern Florida held a small, isolated population of Florida panthers. Its animals showed signs linked to inbreeding: kinked tails, heart defects and poor sperm.

scenes.tts: Put them on the first film's chart. Numbers sit close to the floor. Inbreeding can lower survival, so the gold arrow tilts down. The vortex is turning.
scenes.visual: A TEAL-tinted blue run hovers just above the red-orange floor. The gold arrow tilts downward. The vortex loop beside it spins slowly, its 'more inbreeding' box highlighted. Schematic.
scenes.narration: Put them on the first film's chart. Numbers sit close to the floor. Inbreeding can lower survival, so the gold arrow tilts down. The vortex is turning.

scenes.tts: In nineteen ninety-five, managers tried a genetic rescue. They released eight female pumas from Texas into the Florida population.
scenes.caption: In 1995, managers tried a genetic rescue. They released eight female pumas from Texas into the Florida population.
scenes.visual: On-screen year '1995'. Eight PURPLE puma icons travel from a Texas outline across the map into the TEAL Florida patch. Label 'reinforcement: adding animals to a population that remains'.
scenes.narration: In 1995, managers tried a genetic rescue. They released eight female pumas from Texas into the Florida population.

scenes.tts: Texas pumas belong to the same species, from a separate population. Adding animals to a population that still exists is called reinforcement. The aim was genetic: to reverse inbreeding by bringing in new gene versions.
scenes.visual: Side-by-side cartoons of a TEAL Florida panther and a PURPLE Texas puma with a shared label 'one species, two populations'. A row of gene blocks: the TEAL row mostly identical pairs, PURPLE blocks slotting in to make mixed pairs. Schematic.
scenes.narration: Texas pumas belong to the same species, from a separate population. Adding animals to a population that still exists is called reinforcement. The aim was genetic: to reverse inbreeding by bringing in new gene versions.

scenes.tts: Over the following years, more and more panthers carried both Florida and Texas ancestry. Biologists call such animals admixed.
scenes.visual: A family-tree strip: TEAL and PURPLE parents produce TEAL-PURPLE striped kittens; generation by generation the striped share of the population icons grows. Label 'admixed: both ancestries'. Schematic.
scenes.narration: Over the following years, more and more panthers carried both Florida and Texas ancestry. Biologists call such animals admixed.

scenes.tts: To judge the rescue, track two things. One is the head count. The other is heterozygosity: the share of gene positions where an animal carries two different versions.
scenes.visual: Two gauges appear: 'number of panthers' and 'heterozygosity'. A small inset shows one gene position with two matching blocks (same version) beside one with two differently shaded blocks (two versions). Schematic, labelled blocks only.
scenes.narration: To judge the rescue, track two things. One is the head count. The other is heterozygosity: the share of gene positions where an animal carries two different versions.

scenes.tts: In twenty ten, a team led by Warren Johnson reported the result. Numbers had about tripled. Heterozygosity had doubled. Survival and fitness measures had improved. On the chart, the arrow tilts up.
scenes.caption: In 2010, a team led by Warren Johnson reported the result. Numbers had about tripled. Heterozygosity had doubled. Survival and fitness measures had improved. On the chart, the arrow tilts up.
scenes.visual: On-screen 'Johnson et al., Science, 2010'. The number gauge climbs to 'about 3x', the heterozygosity gauge to '2x'. On the chart, the blue run climbs away from the floor and the gold arrow tilts up.
scenes.narration: In 2010, a team led by Warren Johnson reported the result. Numbers had about tripled. Heterozygosity had doubled. Survival and fitness measures had improved. On the chart, the arrow tilts up.

scenes.tts: The same report warned that habitat loss and persistent inbreeding remained concerns. So, if habitat keeps shrinking, will the climb continue?
scenes.visual: The TEAL patch on the map begins to shrink at its edges, label 'habitat loss'. The chart holds with the run partway up. Question tag: 'will the climb continue?'
scenes.narration: The same report warned that habitat loss and persistent inbreeding remained concerns. So, if habitat keeps shrinking, will the climb continue?

scenes.visual: Hold the frame. Caption 'Predict: does the climb continue?' with a 5-second countdown.

scenes.tts: In twenty twenty-four, a team led by Dave Onorato returned, with records from eleven hundred and ninety-two panthers. The genetic benefits had lasted through five generations.
scenes.caption: In 2024, a team led by Dave Onorato returned, with records from 1,192 panthers. The genetic benefits had lasted through five generations.
scenes.visual: On-screen 'Onorato et al., Scientific Reports, 2024; 1,192 panthers'. The family-tree strip extends to five generations, the striped kittens still marked with a check, label 'benefits through five generations'.
scenes.narration: In 2024, a team led by Dave Onorato returned, with records from 1,192 panthers. The genetic benefits had lasted through five generations.

scenes.tts: Yet the population stabilised, and then declined, during twenty sixteen to twenty twenty. The genetic benefits held, yet the climb stopped. A population gain from genetic rescue may not last if other causes of decline remain.
scenes.caption: Yet the population stabilised, and then declined, during 2016 to 2020. The genetic benefits held, yet the climb stopped. A population gain from genetic rescue may not last if other causes of decline remain.
scenes.visual: On the chart the blue run flattens, then dips, across a shaded band labelled '2016 to 2020: stabilised, then declined'. Beside it a tag 'genetic benefits persist' with a check. Schematic shape, not data.
scenes.narration: Yet the population stabilised, and then declined, during 2016 to 2020. The genetic benefits held, yet the climb stopped. A population gain from genetic rescue may not last if other causes of decline remain.

scenes.tts: How did the teams judge the rescue? They compared admixed with non-admixed animals, and the years after the release with the years before. Both comparisons came from a single population.
scenes.visual: Two comparison panels: left, striped admixed icons beside plain TEAL icons, label 'admixed vs non-admixed'; right, a timeline split at 1995, label 'after vs before'.
scenes.narration: How did the teams judge the rescue? They compared admixed with non-admixed animals, and the years after the release with the years before. Both comparisons came from a single population.

scenes.tts: So genetic rescue can ease inbreeding and lift survival and births. But it does not by itself remove other causes, such as habitat loss or road deaths. Address those too, or the gain may fade. Genes and habitat work together.
scenes.visual: The two cards from the first film reappear: '1. Find and remove the cause of decline' and '2. Alongside: numbers, connections, genes, which can lift the trend or cut the risk'. A PURPLE gene icon drops onto card 2 and the gold arrow lifts; card 1 glows, with the shrinking habitat patch inside it.
scenes.narration: So genetic rescue can ease inbreeding and lift survival and births. But it does not by itself remove other causes, such as habitat loss or road deaths. Address those too, or the gain may fade. Genes and habitat work together.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Take-home line: 'Genes can lift the trend; other causes of decline must still go.'
